items.name: Pearl Harbor Hero Doris Miller Will Stay Namesake of CVN-81
items.summary: The future aircraft carrier CVN-81 will keep its name of USS Doris Miller, USNI News has learned. HII’s Newport News Shipbuilding will lay the ceremonial keel for the future Doris Miller on Dec. 5, according to an invitation to the ceremony reviewed by USNI News. The ship is named after the enlisted sailor who received the Navy Cross for his heroics during the attack on Pearl Harbor. Miller, 25, died in the Battle of Makin.  Earlier this year, CNN reported that the Navy was considering naming CVN-81, potentially in honor of President Donald Trump. items.name: Navy’s 2027 shipbuilding plan would cost $54B a year, federal agency says
items.summary: The Congressional Budget Office released a report Thursday that said the Navy's fiscal 2027 shipbuilding plan will require a roughly $54 billion yearly U.S. investment to complete.
items.full_text:
The Congressional Budget Office released areportThursday breaking down the financial implications of the U.S. Navy’s 2027 plan to invest in more ships and unmanned vessels over the next 30 years.

The federal agency predicted that the annual cost of building ships will hover around $54 billion in 2026 dollars, an 18% uptick from the Navy’s analysis, according to the office.

“CBO estimates that the Navy’s 2027 plan would cost 41 percent more annually in real terms (that is, with costs adjusted to remove the effects of inflation) than the average amount appropriated over the past 5 years,” the report said.

As part of its shipbuilding blueprint, the Navy would increase the number of ships in the fleet from 286 to 398 by 2056; purchase 371 new combat ships and combat logistics and support ships; 58 new and 29 used auxiliary ships; 72 medium unmanned surface vessels; and 15 nuclear-powered guided missile battleships.

But maintenance delays that have plagued the Navy for over a decade would still prevent the Navy from wielding the full offensive capabilities of the vessels if not addressed, the report said.

Extended deployments of ships like the USS Abraham Lincoln, USS Gerald R. Ford and USS Spruance during the Iran war impact vitalmaintenance availabilitywindows for those ships, prolonging the amount of time before they are deployable again.

The CBO quantified that just building new ships would cost an average of $48.9 billion a year, whereas the Navy assessed that construction would cost $41.1 billion.

The CBO also calculated that the annual cost of building new ships stipulated in the 2027 shipbuilding plan is 21% higher than the previous annual cost of the Navy’s 2025 shipbuilding plan.

The increase is due to ships taking longer and being more difficult to build than expected, including elaborate ship designs that run up delays, initial cost estimates for ships that prove incorrect and the introduction of the Navy’s Trump-class battleship program, which ballooned the shipbuilding price tag considerably, according to the agency.

The CBO estimated that the Navy would also spend an additional $4.6 billion a year on other ships not accounted for in the 2027 shipbuilding plan, which only covers new ship construction for battle force ships.

The extra money would cover refueling nuclear-powered ships, outfitting new ships or procuring other vessels that belong to a category outside the battle force.

Part of the 2027 shipbuilding plan includes an increased demand for missile launchers, which would require a massive investment in the military’s munitions stockpile, which hastaken a hitsince the Iran war began.

The CBO appeared to cast doubt that the Navy would be able to fund the ambitious shipbuilding plan, barring an astronomical boost in the service’s yearly stipend.

“Even if the service received annual funding for shipbuilding from 2027 to 2056 that equaled the amount of such funding that it received in each of the past five years — a half-decade during which that funding was at its highest level since the 1980s — the service still could not afford to buy all the ships in its 2027 shipbuilding plan,” the report said.

The DoD submitted the fiscal 2027 shipbuilding plan to Congress on May 11.

If fulfilled, the plan would create the largest Navy fleet since 2001.

Riley Ceder is a reporter at Military Times, where he covers breaking news, criminal justice, investigations, and cyber. He previously worked as an investigative practicum student at The Washington Post, where he contributed to the Abused by the Badge investigation.
